```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)

orders      <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products    <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers     <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")
customers   <- read_csv("data/customers.csv")
```

## The data

The data comes from a Brazilian e-commerce marketplace (the public Olist dataset). I use five of its tables:

| Table | One row is | Why I need it |
|---|---|---|
| orders | one order | status, purchase date, `delivery_days`, `estimated_days` |
| order_items | one item inside an order | price, freight, which seller shipped it |
| products | one product | product weight |
| sellers | one seller | seller state |
| customers | one customer account per order | customer state |

My outcome is `delivery_days`, which lives in the orders table. Every other table is used to describe the order that `delivery_days` belongs to.

## 1. How big is each table?

```{r}
table_sizes <- tibble(
  table   = c("orders", "order_items", "products", "sellers", "customers"),
  rows    = c(nrow(orders), nrow(order_items), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(customers)),
  columns = c(ncol(orders), ncol(order_items), ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(customers))
)

table_sizes
```

**What this told me:** order_items has `r nrow(order_items) - nrow(orders)` more rows than orders, so some orders contain more than one item. customers has exactly as many rows as orders (`r nrow(customers)`), because this dataset creates a new `customer_id` for every order.

**What I did because of it:** since one order can have several item rows, I cannot simply join items onto orders and analyse the result. `delivery_days` is recorded once per order, so I collapse the items to **one row per order** before joining (Section 7).

## 2. What types are the columns?

```{r}
glimpse(orders)
```

**What this told me:** the dates were read as date-times (`dttm`) and `delivery_days` and `estimated_days` are already numeric, so no type conversion is needed. `purchase_year` and `purchase_month` are numbers, which is fine for grouping.

```{r}
glimpse(order_items)
glimpse(products)
```

**What this told me:** `price`, `freight_value` and `product_weight_g` are numeric. The product columns `product_name_lenght` and `product_description_lenght` are misspelled in the source data; I left the names as they are because I do not use those columns.

```{r}
glimpse(sellers)
glimpse(customers)
```

**What this told me:** both tables store location as a two-letter state code (`seller_state`, `customer_state`). I add full state names and regions in Section 8 so the charts are readable.

## 3. Does each ID identify one row?

Before joining, the key columns must be unique in the table they come from. If they were not, a join would silently duplicate rows.

```{r}
key_check <- tibble(
  table        = c("orders", "products", "sellers", "customers"),
  key          = c("order_id", "product_id", "seller_id", "customer_id"),
  rows         = c(nrow(orders), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(customers)),
  unique_keys  = c(n_distinct(orders$order_id), n_distinct(products$product_id),
                   n_distinct(sellers$seller_id), n_distinct(customers$customer_id))
)

key_check
```

**What this told me:** in every table the number of unique keys equals the number of rows, so each ID points to exactly one row.

**What I did because of it:** I can join products, sellers and customers with `left_join()` without creating extra rows. I also checked for fully duplicated rows:

```{r}
duplicate_check <- tibble(
  table          = c("orders", "order_items", "products", "sellers", "customers"),
  duplicate_rows = c(sum(duplicated(orders)), sum(duplicated(order_items)),
                     sum(duplicated(products)), sum(duplicated(sellers)),
                     sum(duplicated(customers)))
)

duplicate_check
```

No table contains fully duplicated rows, so nothing was removed for duplication.

## 4. Where are the missing values?

```{r}
missing_check <- tibble(
  table          = c("orders", "order_items", "products", "sellers", "customers"),
  missing_values = c(sum(is.na(orders)), sum(is.na(order_items)), sum(is.na(products)),
                     sum(is.na(sellers)), sum(is.na(customers)))
)

missing_check
```

Only orders and products have missing values, so I looked at which columns are affected.

### Missing values in orders

```{r}
tibble(
  column         = names(orders),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(orders))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)
```

The missing values are in the delivery date and `delivery_days`, which is my outcome. To find out **why** they are missing, I split them by order status:

```{r}
missing_by_status <- orders |>
  group_by(order_status) |>
  summarise(
    orders                = n(),
    missing_delivery_days = sum(is.na(delivery_days)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(orders))

missing_by_status

delivered_but_missing <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered", is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  nrow()
```

**What this told me:** almost all missing delivery times belong to orders that were never delivered (shipped, canceled, unavailable and so on). Those orders have no delivery time because the delivery never happened. Only `r delivered_but_missing` orders are marked "delivered" but have no delivery date, which looks like a recording error.

**What I did because of it:** I keep only delivered orders with a recorded `delivery_days` (Section 5). I do not fill in the missing values, because inventing a delivery time for an order that never arrived would make the outcome wrong.

### Missing values in products

```{r}
tibble(
  column         = names(products),
  missing_values = colSums(is.na(products))
) |>
  filter(missing_values > 0)
```

**What this told me:** the category and description columns are missing for the same products, but I do not use those columns. Only `r sum(is.na(products$product_weight_g))` products are missing their weight.

**What I did because of it:** I keep all products. Orders that contain one of the products with no weight get a missing shipment weight, and I leave those orders out only of the weight analysis (the count is shown in Section 7).

## 5. Cleaning the orders

```{r}
orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered" & !is.na(delivery_days))

orders_removed <- nrow(orders) - nrow(orders_clean)
```

One `filter()` with `&` keeps a row only when **both** conditions are true: the order was delivered **and** it has a delivery time.

**What this did:** the table went from `r nrow(orders)` to `r nrow(orders_clean)` orders, so `r orders_removed` orders were removed (`r round(orders_removed / nrow(orders) * 100, 1)`% of all orders). They are the undelivered orders and the delivered orders with no delivery date from Section 4.

**Why:** the business question is about how long delivered orders take. An order that never arrived has no delivery time to explain.

Next I checked that the outcome only takes values that make sense:

```{r}
orders_clean |>
  summarise(
    min_delivery_days  = min(delivery_days),
    max_delivery_days  = max(delivery_days),
    zero_day_orders    = sum(delivery_days == 0),
    min_estimated_days = min(estimated_days),
    max_estimated_days = max(estimated_days)
  )
```

**What this told me:** no delivery time is negative, so no order was delivered before it was bought. The `zero_day_orders` column counts same-day deliveries; they are possible for local orders, so I keep them. The maximum is very large, which means there is a long tail of very slow orders. I study that tail on the Exploration page instead of deleting it, because those orders really happened and they are the ones customers complain about.

## 6. Why I do not use "late vs on time" as the outcome

The dataset lets me label each order as on time (delivered within the estimate) or late:

```{r}
orders_clean <- orders_clean |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(delivery_days <= estimated_days, "On Time", "Late")
  )

status_split <- orders_clean |>
  count(delivery_status) |>
  mutate(percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

status_split

on_time_pct <- status_split |> filter(delivery_status == "On Time") |> pull(percent)
```

**What this told me:** `r on_time_pct`% of orders are on time and only `r 100 - on_time_pct`% are late. That imbalance creates two problems:

- A model that always guesses "on time" would already be about `r round(on_time_pct)`% accurate while telling management nothing.
- Every on-time **comparison** gets squeezed. When almost every group is somewhere around `r round(on_time_pct)`% on time, the differences between seller states are only a few percentage points. In a small state a handful of late orders can move its rate as much as a real difference would, so ranking states by on-time rate mostly ranks noise.
- "On time" is measured against the marketplace's own estimate, so the label partly measures how generous the estimate is, not how fast the delivery was.

The second point shows up when I compare the two directly:

```{r}
orders_clean |>
  summarise(
    median_actual_days    = median(delivery_days),
    median_estimated_days = median(estimated_days),
    median_days_early     = median(estimated_days - delivery_days)
  )
```

The typical order arrives well before its estimate, so most orders count as "on time" even when the customer waited a long time.

**What I did because of it:** I use the number `delivery_days` as the single outcome for the project and keep `delivery_status` only as a description. A number keeps the full difference between a 3-day and a 30-day delivery, which the yes/no label throws away. On the Exploration page I compare states with a **boxplot of `delivery_days`**, which does not depend on the on-time split, and I show the late orders separately.

**A note on 92.4% vs 92.6%:** my Milestone 1 Exploration page reported a slightly different on-time rate (92.6%) from this one (92.4%). The difference came from calculating it on the item-level table, where an order with three items was counted three times. Every number from here on is calculated at the order level, so the figures are consistent.

## 7. Building one row per delivered order

`delivery_days` belongs to the order, so every other variable has to be summarised to the order level first.

### Step 1: summarise the items in each order

```{r}
order_summary <- order_items |>
  left_join(products |> select(product_id, product_weight_g, product_category_name), by = "product_id") |>
  group_by(order_id) |>
  summarise(
    n_items            = n(),
    n_sellers          = n_distinct(seller_id),
    seller_id          = first(seller_id),
    order_price        = sum(price),
    order_freight      = sum(freight_value),
    shipment_weight_kg = sum(product_weight_g) / 1000,
    main_category      = first(product_category_name),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(main_category = replace_na(main_category, "unknown"))

order_summary |> count(n_sellers)
```

**What this told me:** almost every order is shipped by a single seller. A few orders contain items from two or more sellers, which means they travel as separate shipments from different places.

**What I did because of it:** for multi-seller orders there is no single seller state to attach `delivery_days` to, so I remove them and report how many (Step 2). `shipment_weight_kg` is missing for any order that contains a product with no weight, because `sum()` returns NA when one part is unknown. That is intentional: I would rather leave the weight missing than understate it. `main_category` is the category of the first item in the order; orders whose product has no category are labelled "unknown" instead of being dropped, because only the category is missing, not the order.

### Step 2: attach the summary, seller and customer to each order

```{r}
orders_with_items <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_summary, by = "order_id")

delivery_data <- orders_with_items |>
  filter(n_sellers == 1) |>
  left_join(sellers |> select(seller_id, seller_state), by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(customers |> select(customer_id, customer_state), by = "customer_id") |>
  mutate(
    same_state    = if_else(seller_state == customer_state, "Same state", "Different state"),
    freight_ratio = order_freight / order_price
  )

rows_check <- tibble(
  step   = c("Delivered orders (cleaned)",
             "Removed: orders with no items",
             "Removed: orders with more than one seller",
             "Final delivery_data"),
  orders = c(nrow(orders_with_items),
             sum(is.na(orders_with_items$n_sellers)),
             sum(orders_with_items$n_sellers > 1, na.rm = TRUE),
             nrow(delivery_data))
)

rows_check
```

This chunk also creates two new variables:

- `same_state` is "Same state" when the seller and the customer are in the same state, otherwise "Different state". It is a rough stand-in for distance.
- `freight_ratio` is the order's freight divided by its price: how much the customer paid in shipping for every 1 real spent on products. A ratio of 0.25 means shipping added 25% on top of the price. Its full summary is in Section 9.

**What this told me:** the final table has one row per delivered, single-seller order. Cleaned orders minus the two removed groups equals the final row count, so the joins did not add or lose any rows by mistake. (`filter(n_sellers == 1)` also drops orders with no items, because their `n_sellers` is NA.)

I also checked that every order found its seller and customer:

```{r}
delivery_data |>
  summarise(
    missing_seller_state   = sum(is.na(seller_state)),
    missing_customer_state = sum(is.na(customer_state)),
    missing_weight         = sum(is.na(shipment_weight_kg))
  )
```

**What this told me:** every order has a seller state and a customer state. Only a handful of orders are missing shipment weight, because of the products with no weight from Section 4. I keep these orders and drop them only from the weight analysis.

## 8. Adding readable state names and regions

Brazil has 27 states (26 states plus the Federal District) grouped into five regions. Region is useful because distance across Brazil is large: shipping from the Southeast to the North is very different from shipping within the Southeast.

```{r}
state_lookup <- tribble(
  ~state, ~state_name,           ~region,
  "AC",   "Acre",                "North",
  "AP",   "Amapá",               "North",
  "AM",   "Amazonas",            "North",
  "PA",   "Pará",                "North",
  "RO",   "Rondônia",            "North",
  "RR",   "Roraima",             "North",
  "TO",   "Tocantins",           "North",
  "AL",   "Alagoas",             "Northeast",
  "BA",   "Bahia",               "Northeast",
  "CE",   "Ceará",               "Northeast",
  "MA",   "Maranhão",            "Northeast",
  "PB",   "Paraíba",             "Northeast",
  "PE",   "Pernambuco",          "Northeast",
  "PI",   "Piauí",               "Northeast",
  "RN",   "Rio Grande do Norte", "Northeast",
  "SE",   "Sergipe",             "Northeast",
  "DF",   "Federal District",    "Center-West",
  "GO",   "Goiás",               "Center-West",
  "MT",   "Mato Grosso",         "Center-West",
  "MS",   "Mato Grosso do Sul",  "Center-West",
  "ES",   "Espírito Santo",      "Southeast",
  "MG",   "Minas Gerais",        "Southeast",
  "RJ",   "Rio de Janeiro",      "Southeast",
  "SP",   "São Paulo",           "Southeast",
  "PR",   "Paraná",              "South",
  "RS",   "Rio Grande do Sul",   "South",
  "SC",   "Santa Catarina",      "South"
)

delivery_data <- delivery_data |>
  left_join(
    state_lookup |> rename(seller_state = state, seller_state_name = state_name, seller_region = region),
    by = "seller_state"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    state_lookup |> rename(customer_state = state, customer_state_name = state_name, customer_region = region),
    by = "customer_state"
  )

delivery_data |>
  summarise(
    unmatched_seller_states   = sum(is.na(seller_state_name)),
    unmatched_customer_states = sum(is.na(customer_state_name))
  )
```

Both counts are 0, so every state code matched the lookup table.

## 9. Descriptive statistics for the key numbers

```{r}
key_stats <- delivery_data |>
  select(delivery_days, estimated_days, order_price, order_freight, freight_ratio, shipment_weight_kg) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(
    count  = n(),
    min    = round(min(value), 2),
    mean   = round(mean(value), 2),
    median = round(median(value), 2),
    max    = round(max(value), 2),
    sd     = round(sd(value), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

key_stats
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dd <- key_stats |> filter(variable == "delivery_days")
fr <- key_stats |> filter(variable == "freight_ratio")
ratio_over_1 <- sum(delivery_data$freight_ratio > 1)
free_freight <- sum(delivery_data$order_freight == 0)
```

**What this told me about `delivery_days`:** the typical (median) order takes `r dd$median` days, but the mean is higher at `r dd$mean` days and the maximum is `r dd$max` days. A mean above the median means the distribution has a long right tail: a minority of very slow orders pulls the average up.

**What I did because of it:** on the Exploration page I compare groups using the **median** and boxplots, which are not distorted by the slow tail, and I show the tail separately.

### Text columns: how many orders in each level

```{r}
delivery_data |> count(seller_region, sort = TRUE)
delivery_data |> count(customer_region, sort = TRUE)
delivery_data |> count(same_state, sort = TRUE)
delivery_data |> count(purchase_day_of_week, sort = TRUE)
delivery_data |> count(main_category, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pct_cross <- round(mean(delivery_data$same_state == "Different state") * 100, 1)
top_seller_region <- delivery_data |> count(seller_region, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1)
top_customer_region <- delivery_data |> count(customer_region, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1)
```

**What this told me:** the largest seller region is the `r top_seller_region$seller_region` (`r round(top_seller_region$n / nrow(delivery_data) * 100, 1)`% of orders) and the largest customer region is the `r top_customer_region$customer_region` (`r round(top_customer_region$n / nrow(delivery_data) * 100, 1)`%). `r pct_cross`% of orders cross a state line. The top 10 categories show how concentrated the product mix is; "unknown" is the group of products with no category.

**What I did because of it:** regions with few orders get their own minimum-size rule on the Exploration page, so small groups are not compared as if they were as reliable as the Southeast.

### How to read `freight_ratio`

`freight_ratio` = order freight ÷ order price. It tells you how much the customer pays in shipping **for every 1 real spent on products**. I calculate it once per order (total freight ÷ total price) instead of averaging item-level ratios as I did in Milestone 1. Averaging item ratios gives a 1-real item the same weight as a 1,000-real item, which does not match what the customer paid for the whole order.

- **Median `r fr$median`**: for a typical order, shipping adds about `r round(fr$median * 100)` cents per 1 real of product, roughly `r round(fr$median * 100)`% on top of the price.
- **Mean `r fr$mean` vs median `r fr$median`**: the mean is above the median, so the distribution is skewed to the right. A minority of orders with very high shipping relative to price pulls the average up.
- **SD `r fr$sd`**: the standard deviation is large compared with the median, so the ratio varies a lot from order to order.
- **Maximum `r fr$max`**: this is a single order, which paid `r fr$max` times its product price in shipping (a very cheap item). One order says nothing about the typical order, so I do not read the maximum as a pattern.
- `r ratio_over_1` orders (`r round(ratio_over_1 / nrow(delivery_data) * 100, 1)`%) paid more for shipping than for the products (`freight_ratio` above 1), and `r free_freight` orders had free shipping (ratio of 0).

**What I did because of it:** I keep the extreme ratios because they are real orders. I use the median when comparing groups, and on the Exploration page I check whether a high freight ratio goes together with slower delivery.

## 10. Final dataset

```{r}
delivery_data <- delivery_data |>
  select(
    order_id, delivery_days, estimated_days, delivery_status,
    purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_day_of_week,
    seller_state, seller_state_name, seller_region,
    customer_state, customer_state_name, customer_region, same_state,
    n_items, main_category, order_price, order_freight, freight_ratio, shipment_weight_kg
  )

dim(delivery_data)
```

The final dataset has **`r nrow(delivery_data)` delivered orders** (one row each) and `r ncol(delivery_data)` columns.

| Variable | Meaning | Known when the order is placed? |
|---|---|---|
| `delivery_days` | days from purchase to delivery (**outcome**) | No, this is what we want to predict |
| `estimated_days` | days the marketplace promised | Yes |
| `delivery_status` | on time / late | No, it is calculated from the outcome |
| `purchase_year`, `purchase_month`, `purchase_day_of_week` | when the order was placed | Yes |
| `seller_state`, `seller_region` | where the seller ships from | Yes |
| `customer_state`, `customer_region` | where the customer lives | Yes |
| `same_state` | seller and customer in the same state | Yes |
| `n_items` | items in the order | Yes |
| `main_category` | product category of the first item | Yes |
| `order_price`, `order_freight`, `freight_ratio` | money paid for products and shipping | Yes |
| `shipment_weight_kg` | total product weight | Yes |

The last column matters for Milestone 2. A model may only use information that exists when the order is placed. `delivery_status` and the delivery date are calculated from the outcome itself, so they are excluded from modeling.

I save the table so the Exploration page uses exactly the same data:

```{r}
write_rds(delivery_data, "data/delivery_data.rds")
```

The file is saved inside `data/`, which is excluded from GitHub, so no data is uploaded to the repository.
